 Commentary: Democrats should raise the minimum wage
 Published 10:00 am Friday, November 13, 2026
 By Michael Hiltzik/Los Angeles Times, TNS 
 Illinois Governor JB Pritzker speaks onstage during the Clinton Global Initiative 2026 Annual Meeting at New York Hilton Midtown on September 22, 2026 in New York City. 
 (JP Yim/Getty Images for Clinton Global Initiative, TNS) 
 Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... 
 The newly Democratic Congress faces a lengthy agenda once it’s sworn in on Jan. 3 — reversing cuts in Medicare and Medicaid, reestablishing premium subsidies for Affordable Care Act health plans, holding President Donald Trump’s incompetent cabinet members to account, investigating the self-dealing and corruption of this White House, etc., etc.
 But there is an obvious initial fix for the economic pain suffered by ordinary Americans that falls into the issue of “affordability,” which drove much of the pivot away from Republicans in last week’s midterm voting: raise the federal minimum wage.
 Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker named that reform as “an easy way to start” in advancing the Democrats’ economic agenda during a post-election appearance on CNN.
 He’s right. The federal minimum has been frozen at $7.25 an hour since June 2009. Accounting for inflation, that figure has shrunk to $4.64 in buying power; putting it another way, if it were adjusted for inflation, it would be $11.33 today.
 “You can’t survive on $14,000 a year with a single full-time job,” Pritzker told CNN’s Kaitlin Collins. (Actually, $7.25 an hour at 40 hours a week would be about $15,000 over 52 weeks, but of course minimum wage laborers are especially vulnerable to lost working hours through furloughs and layoffs and generalized stinginess of employers.)
 The federal minimum wage has long ranked as our most persistent relic of the economic past. Again in inflation-adjusted terms, its value peaked in 1968, when it was $1.60, or $15.81 in 2026 dollars.
 It’s not as if Congress is insensitive to the ravages of inflation. The lawmakers last raised their own pay with a 2.8% raise to $174,000, effective in January 2009, six months before they enacted the last minimum wage increase.
 Pritzker’s conjecture that raising the federal minimum would be a relatively easy fix is because so many other economic reforms will be saddled with political complexities and focused opposition. That’s not to say that raising the federal minimum wouldn’t run into any opposition. Commercial and industrial lobbies always have disdained the minimum wage, asserting that it suppresses hiring to the point where it costs average workers more than they gain. 
 The labor effects of the minimum wage are among the most heavily researched by economists. Their findings range widely, which suggests that they’re not very substantial. In 2019, the Congressional Budget Office, that nonpartisan judge of federal policy, reckoned that raising the minimum wage to $15 by 2025 would “boost the wages of 17 million workers who would otherwise earn less than $15 per hour,” and that 10 million workers earning slightly more than $15 per hour might also receive a raise.
 About 1.3 million other workers would lose their jobs, according to what CBO called its median estimate. Overall, the population of those with income below the poverty line would fall by 1.3 million.
 The CBO also cautioned, however, that there was a two-thirds chance “the change in employment would be between about zero and a decrease of 3.7 million workers.” Put it all together, and the CBO study provided grist both for both the pro and con camps.
 The advocates of a higher minimum wage have justice and economics on their side. The opponents largely have myths, the union-affiliated Economic Policy Institute maintains.
 There’s virtually no evidence that a higher minimum contributes meaningfully to inflation: The $20 fast-food minimum wage in California raised prices about 2.1%, or 8 cents on a $4 order, in the first six months after its implementation while increasing average weekly raises by 12% without reducing employment, University of California economists Denis Sosinskiy and Michael Reich reported in May 2025. Nor is it true that most minimum-wage workers are teenagers on their first jobs, as opponents typically assert. 
 But the anti-poverty effects of raising the minimum are hard to dispute and have been supported by the CBO’s analysis, among others.
 Michael Hiltzik is a columnist for The Los Angeles Times.
